old: and his people prosper under him
new: and his people do good deeds under him
reason: Butler: “and his people do good deeds under him” — the draft turns the people’s moral conduct into material prosperity, although the drafter’s notes say this clause was kept.

old: yet see how he alone has kept you from ever getting back to your own home
new: yet see how, of all men, you are the only one he has kept from ever getting back to your own home
reason: Butler: “yet see how he has prevented you alone from ever getting back to your own home” — “alone” is on Odysseus (he alone of all is kept from home), and the draft moves it onto Zeus (“he alone”), which changes the complaint.

old: to set up a great loom in my room and start on a huge piece of fine weaving
new: to set up a great embroidery frame in my room and start on a huge piece of fine needlework
reason: Butler: “a great tambour-frame … an enormous piece of fine needlework”, the same words as at B02-P005, which accepted Book 2 (candidate-v6) prints as “a great embroidery frame … fine needlework”. The notes’ statement that there was “no prior GLOSSARY row” misses that accepted precedent, and “loom/weaving” changes the craft Butler names.

old: because I wouldn’t want my skill at weaving to go to waste—until I’ve finished a shroud for old Laertes
new: because I wouldn’t want my skill in needlework to perish unrecorded—until I’ve finished a pall for the hero Laertes
reason: Butler: “for I would not have my skill in needlework perish unrecorded—till I have finished making a pall for the hero Laertes”, word for word the speech at B02-P005, which accepted Book 2 prints as “skill in needlework perish unrecorded … a pall for the hero Laertes”. The draft drops “hero”, adds “old”, and changes “pall” to “shroud” and “perish unrecorded” to “go to waste”.

old: if he were laid out without a shroud.’
new: if he were laid out without a pall.’
reason: Butler: “laid out without a pall”; accepted B02-P005: “laid out without a pall.” This goes with the previous finding, so that one object has one name within the speech and across the Books.

old: I suppose Odysseus’ hands
new: I suppose Odysseus’s hands
reason: GLOSSARY hazard 3: the possessive is “Odysseus’s”, and the build asserts that no bare “Odysseus’” survives. Butler has “Ulysses’ hands”.

old: bound up Odysseus’ wound
new: bound up Odysseus’s wound
reason: GLOSSARY hazard 3 (the “Odysseus’s” possessive, build-asserted). Butler has “bound Ulysses’ wound”.

old: When the child of morning, rosy-fingered Dawn, appeared,
new: When Dawn, the rosy-fingered child of morning, appeared,
reason: Butler: “When the child of morning, rosy-fingered Dawn, appeared”. The GLOSSARY dawn row and ODY-RULES fix the edition form as “When Dawn, the rosy-fingered child of morning, appeared,”, and every accepted Book prints it that way (B10-P13, B12-P1, B13-P2, B15-P15, B17-P0). The draft keeps Butler’s order.

old: since they’re no longer what they were when Odysseus went away, but have become stained and blackened with soot. Add especially that you’re afraid Zeus might set them quarreling over their wine, and that they might do each other some harm that would disgrace both the feast and the wooing,
new: since they’re no longer what they were when Odysseus left, but have become stained and blackened with soot. Add especially that you’re afraid Zeus might make them quarrel over their wine and harm each other, which would disgrace both the feast and the courtship,
reason: From “say that you have taken it” to “tempts people to use them”, Butler is word-identical to B16-P27, where Odysseus gives this instruction in advance. The notes say the B16 wording is reused, but only part of it is: the draft differs in “went away”/“left”, “set them quarreling … and that they might do each other some harm that would disgrace”/“make them quarrel … and harm each other, which would disgrace”, and “wooing”/“courtship”. This matches accepted B16 exactly. The draft’s wording is itself closer to Butler, so the alternative is a B16 successor, but the echo should be one wording.

old: shut the women up in their rooms
new: shut the women up in their room
reason: Butler: “shut the women up in their room”, singular, as the draft’s own ¶4 (“bolted the women into their room”) has it.

old: looking as lovely as Aphrodite or Artemis
new: looking like Aphrodite or Artemis
reason: Butler: “looking like Venus or Diana”, with no “lovely”. Accepted B17-P3 renders the same formula “looking like Artemis or Aphrodite”.

old: I can see exactly how badly you’re behaving
new: I can see how disgracefully you’re behaving
reason: Butler: “I see how abominably you are behaving”. “badly” softens Penelope’s anger, and “exactly” is added.

old: her chief waiting-woman, Eurynome
new: her chief waiting woman, Eurynome
reason: Accepted B17-P50 prints “her waiting woman Eurynome” open, and PUNCTUATION §4 (compound drift) requires one setting across the Books.

old: who on the whole face of the earth could find fault with you? Your fame reaches all the way to heaven, like that of some blameless king who upholds justice,
new: who on the whole face of the earth would dare to find fault with you? Your fame reaches all the way to heaven; you are like some blameless king who upholds justice,
reason: Butler: “who … can dare to chide with you? Your fame reaches the firmament of heaven itself; you are like some blameless king”. The draft drops “dare” and compares her fame to the king’s fame, where Butler compares Penelope herself to the king.

old: the ewes bear lambs without fail, and the sea teems with fish, all because of his good rule,
new: the ewes bear lambs, and the sea teems with fish, all because of his virtues,
reason: Butler: “the ewes bring forth lambs, and the sea abounds with fish by reason of his virtues”. “without fail” is added, and “good rule” replaces the moral quality (virtues) that the next clause (“do good deeds”) builds on.

old: when the fourth year came round, as the seasons turned and many days had passed, those worthless maids of mine gave me away
new: when I was in my fourth year, as the moons waned and many days went by, those good-for-nothing hussies, my maids, gave me away
reason: Butler: “as time wore on and I was now in my fourth year, in the waning of moons, and many days had been accomplished, those good for nothing hussies my maids betrayed me”. The draft replaces the waning moons with “seasons” and softens “hussies”, a word it keeps at ¶20.

old: at night I’d unpick it again by torchlight
new: at night I’d unpick the stitches again by torchlight
reason: Butler: “unpick the stitches again by torch light”, and accepted B02-P006: “unpick the stitches again by torchlight”.

old: I, being the younger, was called Aethon; my brother was both the older and the braver of the two. It was in Crete
new: I, the younger, am called Aethon; my brother, though, was both the older and the braver of the two. So it was in Crete
reason: Butler: “I, who am the younger, am called Aethon; my brother, however, was at once the older and the more valiant of the two; hence it was in Crete”. The draft moves the name he gives into the past tense and drops the causal “hence”: he stayed in Crete because his brother had gone.

old: so carefully did he hold back his own tears
new: so cunningly did he hold back his tears
reason: Butler: “so cunningly did he restrain his tears”. “carefully” loses the guile, and “own” is added.

old: And I’ll say this too, and mean it seriously: I don’t know whether
new: Furthermore I say—and take my words to heart—I don’t know whether
reason: Butler: “Furthermore I say, and lay my saying to your heart, that I do not know”. The formula asks the listener to take the words in, not the speaker to mean them. Accepted B11-P37 and B16-P27 print “Furthermore I say—and take my words to heart—”.

old: since he thought the most like Odysseus himself
new: since he was the most like-minded with him
reason: Butler: “as being the most like-minded with himself”. The draft’s clause does not parse aloud (“he thought the most like”).

old: don’t wear yourself down any further grieving
new: don’t spoil your looks any further by grieving
reason: Butler: “do not disfigure yourself further by grieving”. The concern is for her looks (cf. ¶13, “robbed me of all my beauty”), not her strength.

old: answered Penelope, “if your words come true
new: answered Penelope. “If your words come true
reason: Butler: “answered Penelope; “if your words…”. PUNCTUATION §3 normalizes comma-continuation to a full stop and capital, and as drafted “May it be even so, if your words come true …” runs the wish into the condition.

old: I’ve foresworn rugs
new: I’ve forsworn rugs
reason: Butler’s “foresworn” is a nonstandard spelling. The modern standard form is “forsworn”.

old: none has ever spoken with such admirable good sense as you
new: none has ever spoken in all things with such admirable propriety as you
reason: Butler: “there never was one who spoke in all things with such admirable propriety”. The draft drops “in all things” and replaces propriety (fitness of speech) with good sense.

old: took the basin she meant to wash his feet in
new: took the cauldron she meant to wash his feet in
reason: Butler: “took the cauldron in which she was going to wash his feet”. Accepted B10-P28 keeps “cauldron” for a bath vessel, and the house rule is not to generalize concrete nouns.

old: the most accomplished thief and liar in the whole world
new: the most accomplished thief and perjurer in the whole world
reason: Butler: “the most accomplished thief and perjurer”. Perjury (false oaths) is a specific skill, which is Hermes’s gift in the next sentence. The drafter’s notes say “perjurer” was kept.

old: so call the child Odysseus, the child of anger.
new: so name the child ‘Odysseus,’ or the child of anger.
reason: Butler: “so name the child ‘Ulysses,’ or the child of anger”. This is the only paragraph whose “ ” ‘ counts differ from the source (2/2/1 against 2/2/0): the draft drops the single quotes that mark the name as a word, and the “or” that introduces its meaning. The notes say the gloss was kept “exactly as Butler frames it”.

old: how he had come to be hurt
new: how he had come by the scar
reason: Butler: “how he had hurt himself to get the scar”. The scar is what the whole digression explains, and the draft’s final sentence of the story drops it.

old: I’d like to speak with you a little longer about another matter
new: I’d like to speak with you briefly about another matter
reason: Butler: “I should like to speak with you briefly about another matter”. “a little longer” is a different claim from “briefly”.

old: And I’ll say this too, and take it to heart—the coming dawn
new: Furthermore I say—and take my words to heart—the coming dawn
reason: Butler: “Furthermore I say—and lay my saying to your heart—”, the exact form accepted B11-P37 prints as “Furthermore I say—and take my words to heart—”. It should also match ¶16.

old: Those that come through the gate of ivory are deceptive
new: Those that come through the gate of ivory are empty
reason: Butler: “Those that come through the gate of ivory are fatuous, but those from the gate of horn mean something”. The contrast is empty against meaningful, and “deceptive” adds deceit.

old: watch that you don’t fall out of favor with your mistress, and that Odysseus doesn’t come home, for there’s still a chance he may.
new: watch that you don’t fall out of favor with your mistress—and beware of Odysseus coming home, for there’s still a chance he may.
reason: As written, 'watch that you don't fall out of favor... and that Odysseus doesn't come home' reads as two parallel instructions the maid must obey (don't lose favor; prevent Odysseus's return), which is backwards — Odysseus is warning her that his return is the thing that will expose her bad behavior. A listener hearing this once will likely parse it as telling the maid to keep Odysseus away, the opposite of the intended threat. [lead: Butler gives two separate warnings (“lest… and lest”); the proposed merge changed the meaning]

old: got subscriptions of wine and oxen so they could sacrifice as much as they liked
new: got contributions of wine and oxen for them so they could sacrifice as much as they liked
reason: 'Subscriptions' now means a recurring paid service (a magazine or streaming subscription); the older sense of 'collected contributions from the community' will actively mislead a modern listener rather than just sound quaint. [lead: no added “from my neighbors”]

old: carrying him off course from Cape Malea and leaving him at Amnisus, off the cave of Ilithuia, where the harbors are hard to enter and he could barely find shelter from the storm then raging
new: carrying him off course from Cape Malea to Amnisus, near the cave of Ilithuia, where the harbors are hard to enter; he could barely find shelter there from the storm that was raging
reason: One sentence stacks four place names and clauses (off course from X, leaving him at Y, off the cave of Z, where the harbors..., he could barely find shelter) with no breaks; heard aloud it is hard to keep the geography straight even though no single fact is confusing on its own. Splitting the final clause into its own sentence lets a listener land each piece before the next arrives.

old: the ship was ready by the water and the crew found who would take Odysseus to his own country
new: the ship was ready by the water and the crew was found who would take Odysseus to his own country
reason: The second clause drops the auxiliary ('crew found' instead of 'crew was found'), so on first hearing 'the crew found' sounds like the crew is the one doing the finding, and the listener has to backtrack when 'who would take Odysseus' arrives. Restoring 'was' removes the false start without changing the meaning.

old: and he had enough lying in King Pheidon’s house to keep his family for ten generations
new: and Odysseus had enough of it lying in King Pheidon’s house to keep his own family for ten generations
reason: The subject of the sentence up to this point is Pheidon ('he showed me... and he had enough...'), so 'he' and 'his family' read as continuing to refer to Pheidon, when the treasure and family in question are Odysseus's. A listener will likely attach the wealth to the wrong man.

old: Hermes himself had endowed him with this gift, for he used to burn the thighbones of goats and kids to him, and so the god took pleasure in his company.
new: Hermes himself had given Autolycus this gift, for Autolycus used to burn the thighbones of goats and kids in offering to him, and so the god took pleasure in his company.
reason: Four pronouns in one sentence (him/he/him/his) swap back and forth between Autolycus and Hermes with only 'the god' at the very end to anchor one of them; a listener has no way to track who is receiving the gift, who is burning the offerings, and who is being honored until the sentence is already over. Naming Autolycus once resolves the chain without adding any fact not already in the text.

old: like the stays on which a ship is built
new: like the props a ship is built on
reason: 'Stays' today means the rigging cables that hold up a mast; a listener picturing sailing rigging will misread the image of axes lined up like a ship's foundation supports. 'Timbers' keeps the same building-frame image without the false sailing association. [lead: Butler “stays” = supports/props]
